items.title: The US pastor who wants to see women's right to vote overturned
items.summary: The movement to repeal women's right to vote has gained traction amongst some very conservative Christians.
items.content:
"Patriarchy is in accordance with the way God made the world." That is the view of Pastor Doug Wilson, a conservative minister who the US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth calls his mentor.

Speaking to the BBC from his base in Moscow, Idaho, Wilson explained his view that a society led by men is "a very great blessing". It's a perspective Christians who disagree with him say is based on a fundamentalist understanding of the Bible, which promotes the subjugation of women.

A self-described Christian nationalist, Wilson believes the US should be a theocracy, with gay sex criminalised, abortion outlawed, and people of other faiths unable to hold public office.

In the past he has delivered a sermon on "The Lost Virtue of Sexism," arguing that the Bible says women should be excluded from leadership of the church, and certain roles in civic affairs. And as part of his views on the division between the sexes, he would like the 19th Amendment of the US constitution, which granted women the right to vote, to be repealed, something his detractors say is anti-democratic.

The vast majority of Christians support women's right to vote, and dismiss his message as misogynistic and extreme.

Rev. Canon Dana Colley Corsello, the vicar at the Washington National Cathedral, rejects Wilson's understanding of what the Bible says about women's roles.

"In my mind, there is no biblical precedent or standing for what [Wilson has] proposed," she told the BBC.

"I'm married, I have a husband, I have children. My husband and I are complete equals in everything we do."

Have the American Pope and the American administration fallen out?

Pete Hegseth brings combative style as face of Trump's war in Iran

But while Wilson still represents a fringe perspective amongst Christians in the US, some of his views have been gaining support.

The denomination he co-founded, the Communion of Reformed Evangelical Churches (CREC), has around 150 churches in the US. It's a drop in the ocean compared to the 350,000 or so other Christian congregations the US. But Wilson says membership continues to rise.

His influence has grown in part because of his connection to Pete Hegseth. The Secretary of Defence is a "proud member" of a CREC affiliated church, a Pentagon spokesperson told the BBC, adding that the "secretary very much appreciates many of Mr. Wilson's writings and teachings".

Wilson says the two have "a warm relationship", although he stresses it is "largely a pastoral one, not a political one". Wilson has led prayer services at the Pentagon, including one in mid-November.

Joining Wilson on stage, Pete Hegseth said "thank you for your leadership, for your mentorship, for the things you've started, the truth you've told, your willingness to be bold."

Hegseth worships at the Washington, DC branch of Wilson's network of churches. And there are other members of the current administration that worship there too, according to Wilson.

Of all his views, it is his statements on women's suffrage that have garnered the most headlines.

Wilson favours "household voting", where the head of the home – usually a man – votes on behalf of their family. It's the system used for elections within his church, although the women in Wilson's family do vote in civic elections in order to counter votes of liberals, he says.

He says only in "odd" circumstances, such as divorce or bereavement or "where the husband was a quadriplegic," should women assume the role of head of household. Just 7% of votes in Wilson's church polity are cast by women.

When challenged by the BBC, he admitted it was a system that gave men "outsized influence".

Wilson says that repealing the 19th Amendment is "low" on the list of priorities for him and his congregation. But, he adds, "we do think it".

Julie Ingersoll, a professor of religious studies at the University of North Florida, says Wilson's beliefs are misogynistic and extreme - part of a world view that says women should be in complete submission to men in every part of their lives.

It is extremely unlikely that the 19th Amendment would be repealed - it would require either a proposal from two-thirds of the House and Senate or two-thirds of the state legislatures. Three quarters of states would then need to ratify it.

Still, says Ingersoll, the threat to women's rights should be taken seriously.

"It's not unlike the battle that they waged against Roe versus Wade," she says, referencing the Supreme Court decision that granted women the right to an abortion. It was overturned in 2022, after years of legal battles that restricted women's access to abortion.

"Thirty years ago, people would have said, oh, they're not gonna undo abortion rights.

"But they chipped away and they kept chipping away until they were able to overturn it. And I see this as directly parallel."

While Wilson says overturning the 19th Amendment could take a century or more, there are conservative Christians who are pushing for women to have their right to vote removed more immediately.

Last February, pastor Dale Partridge posted on Instagram saying "We will repeal the 19th Amendment within ten years".

Partridge, who has around 900k followers across social media, credits Wilson as being someone who "broke the ice" for "strong politics and theology".

Partridge has said that "the majority of women are not capable of responsible voting" because too many of them are liberal.

He also frequently collaborates on podcasts with another conservative pastor named Joel Webbon.

Webbon, whose New Christian Right YouTube channel has more than 190k subscribers, has said that women's "desires are wicked". The solution, he claims, is to "take away women's vote". He was once friendly with Wilson, although they have since fallen out.

"Those guys have overshot by a long way," says Wilson of the two younger pastors. "They are disruptors and basically rage baiting."

Kelly Marino, an associate professor at Sacred Heart University who studies women's suffrage, says that the last decade has seen big wins for the women's rights movement, and "liberal political ideology" in general.

But, she argues, "any time where there was sort of this peak of feminism, there've been people who respond aggressively and try to push back".

Added to that are the high levels of uncertainty and conflict that have characterised the post-Covid period.

"I think there's been this craving for tradition and things that felt safe," Marino says.

That, she says, can be seen in the popularity of notions such as being a "tradwife" or "soft girl", who reject career goals in favour of traditionally female roles of wife and mother.

Marino says that while she doesn't think the constitution could be changed in the immediate future, the conversation around repealing the 19th Amendment is shaping the way people think about women's roles in general.

Canon Corsello, the Vicar at Washington Cathedral, sees the midterm election results as a repudiation of the push against women's rights.

"Cultural issues did not translate in this election", she says. "When people are preaching love, empathy, inclusion... that actually resonated with people".

Wilson's views have, however, been gaining ground beyond the US. The CREC has more than 30 churches internationally, including in Poland, Japan and Brazil.

The latter country has seen its own movement of right-wing influencers pressing for the removal of women's suffrage, with some leaning on religious language to make their point.

Wilson wants to continue expanding his brand of Christianity around the world, and has recently accepted a church in England into his network.

While CREC churches in each country have their own distinct characteristics, Wilson says their core beliefs are the same.

When it comes to the US, he says his ideal scenario would be for his congregations to "to practice what we believe in the church and for outsiders to look at that and envy it and say, man, that seems like a good system".

Hegseth awards medal to war memorial guard who reprimanded him and group

'It's a farce': Hegseth's defiant response to impeachment effort

items.title: Spanish elections: What you need to know and what's at stake
items.summary: After eight years of Socialist-led rule, snap elections are taking place on Sunday with conservative Alberto Núñez Feijóo vying to win office.
items.content:
After eight years of Socialist-led government under Pedro Sánchez, Spain is at a crossroads.

Snap elections are taking place on Sunday 29 November, and voters face a choice of continued left-wing rule or a conservative-led government, with the likely support of far-right Vox.

Alberto Núñez Feijóo's conservative People's Party is narrowly ahead of the Socialist PSOE in most polls.

He has spoken of Spain being probably at "the most significant moment in our country for the past 50 years", and he aims to "repair the state, regenerate democracy, reunited the nation and recover Spain's ambition and self-esteem". But it is unlikely he could do anything without the backing of Vox, who are third in the opinion polls.

For more on Feijóo and who else to watch in this election - read here .

Spain has a population of almost 50 million, and almost 39 million people have the right to vote for the Congress and the upper house, the Senate. The polls open at 09:00 (08:00 GMT) on Sunday and close at 20:00 (19:00 GMT), when the first exit polls come out.

Sánchez called this vote eight months early after MPs rejected planned changes to Spain's housing laws.

He was responding to nationwide protests after an 87-year-old woman called Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her rented flat in Madrid and later died.

But his government lost the support of a centre-right party called Junts from the north-eastern region of Catalonia which sought to protect the rights of property owners.

Housing remains one of the hot-button issues for voters, but they are also focused on the high cost of living, corruption and immigration.

Spain's property prices and rents have soared by more than 80% from 2015 to 2025, and wages have not kept pace.

Spain has a combination of high demand and scarce supply: the Bank of Spain estimates 700,000 homes are needed to ease the pressure.

The result is that millions of Spaniards have little chance to buy a house, while they live in fear of eviction if their rent is increased. On 11 November, four million Spaniards were galvanised into joining the first general strike since 2012, according to the unions.

Pedro Sánchez has embraced housing reform as a big campaign issue and left-wing parties have promised rent controls and protection against eviction, while the right is focusing on building more homes, tax breaks for homebuyers and planning deregulation.

Support for the Socialists is down from 2023, but even then he came second in the race and relied on the backing of other parties, mainly on the left, to stay in power. This time those other left-wing parties, in particular the Broad Front (Frente Amplio) have fallen back and the big questions now are more about Feijóo's conservatives.

"It is a demobilisation of the left. Sanchez's party is not doing well," says Jacobo Ramos Folch, Policy Analyst and visiting professor at the University of Navarra.

"That lack of majority is really a reality – and the rise of Vox. What is changing that shift of majorities is the rise of Vox."

Vox have been around since 2013 but polls suggest this time they could almost double their 33 seats in Spain's lower house, the Congress.

Their big themes are "national priority" – putting Spanish citizens first for subsidies and welfare, along with repatriating migrants "in an illegal situation" and "remigration" of foreigners who do not contribute to Spain.

Migration has become a key challenge for Spain, and Alberto Nuñez Feijoo has accused his rival of being a "problem for Europe when it comes to immigration" after the influx of tens of thousands of migrants into the exclave of Ceuta from neighbouring Morocco in July.

This month too, the Canary Island of El Hierro has seen record arrivals, with 2,000 people landing there on 24 November. Abascal has spoken of "another invasion".

And yet a recent CIS survey put it far behind housing, cost of living, healthcare and working conditions.

The PP and Vox have bitterly criticised the Socialist-led government for a drive to legalise unauthorised migrants this year that attracted 1.2 million applications.

Feijóo's party wants to see more controlled immigration. Vox has called for mass deportations.

Clashing political visions reflect a divided Spain ahead of election

Feijóo has accused the Socialists of being "the most corrupt party" that Spain had ever seen, and a number of cases have involved Sánchez's inner circle and family.

People should distinguish between real and "fictitious" corruption allegations, says el momento más trascendental.

His former transport minister José Luis Ábalos has been given 24 years in prison over multiple corruption offences.

Leading party figure Santos Cerdán awaits trial for alleged bribery and denies wrongdoing.

Sánchez's wife Begoña Gómez faces trial for alleged misuse of public funds and using her marriage to further her academic career. She denies wrongdoing. And his brother David Sánchez has been banned from public office for nine years for administrative misconduct.

Feijóo has made clear his objective is to form a majority and make "parliamentary support agreements" with Vox. As far as a coalition is concerned, he says he will respect the will of Spanish voters, but maintains Abascal has never talked to him about running any ministries.

The PP leader is clear that Vox's national priority policy would run counter to Spain's constitution and European Union treaties: "No-one can sign illegal agreements."

Even if they were to go into coalition, Camino Mortera-Martinez of the Centre for European Reform, and a former European affairs adviser to the Spanish prime minister is not convinced Vox would wield much influence.

"They're not going to get any of the core ministries. They're not going to get defence or home affairs or foreign policy or economy," she told the BBC. Even if they take over the education ministry, Mortera-Martinez argues education policy is largely devolved to Spain's regional governments.

Since 2022, Vox has worked with the PP in a series of regional coalition governments, holding ministries such as culture and tourism. At the time Feijóo had reservations about Vox joining the conservatives in government in Castilla y León.

The following year they went into coalition with the conservatives in Valencia, Aragón, Murcia, and Extremadura, but pulled out of all five governments in 2024 when they refused to accept unaccompanied migrant children being moved to their regions.

They have since signed new coalition pacts with the PP in Extremadura, Aragón, Castilla y León and Andalusia.

Unlike many European countries Spain has 17 autonomous communities (and two cities) that have their own parliament and their own powers. Catalonia in the north-east and the Basque Country in the north have their own police forces.

The regions matter to Sunday's result. Catalonia alone has 48 seats out of the 350 in Spain's parliament, and the Socialists have recently come to rely on regional parties for support.

Sánchez's government relied on the support of Basque separatists Bildu and two Catalan parties, ERC on the left and Junts on the right. But when Junts refused to back his housing reform, he decided to dissolve parliament.

Spain is made up of 50 constituencies which each have a minimum of two seats.

The exclaves of Ceuta and Melilla both have one, and the other 248 seats are divided proportionally according to voter numbers.

Madrid province will have 38 seats, Barcelona 32 and Valencia 16.

To win a seat, a party has to win 3% of the vote in a province, but in smaller provinces with fewer seats parties generally need more than that.

items.title: France's political mainstream risks presidential vote debacle with no clear candidate
items.summary: Hard-right and hard-left candidates dominate the polls ahead of next year's presidential election.
items.content:
France's political mainstream faces wipe-out at the presidential election in April-May 2027, unless it acts fast to choose who it wishes to stand.

With every poll confirming the dominance of hard-right and hard-left leaders Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon, candidates of the middle-ground – the old "legacy" parties – are being squeezed out of the game.

In theory any contender from centre-right or centre-left who was chosen in the first multi-candidate round of voting in April should be in a strong position to win in the play-off a fortnight later.

That is because at their separate ends of the spectrum both Le Pen and Mélenchon have more people who oppose than support them.

But personal rivalries, lack of preparation and differing political visions have so far put paid to any hope of a meaningful challenge.

"The game in the centre is totally blocked," says political writer François Fressoz at the left-leaning Le Monde newspaper. "The partisans of reason have lost their reason."

On the left – the old Socialist Party and its acolytes – there is at least agreement on a candidate: European Parliament MP Raphaël Glucksmann.

His problem is that allies who he might once have counted on – Greens, Communists and other small left-wing parties, not to mention many Socialist voters – are being pulled inexorably into the Mélenchon orbit.

In the last two weeks, Green party leader Marine Tondelier, a majority of Communist parliamentary deputies and one-time Socialist presidential hopeful Benoît Hamon have all thrown in their lot with the leader of France Unbowed (LFI).

Another prominent figure of the left – François Ruffin – has also withdrawn from the race, bowing to the unbowed Mélenchon's now almost total command of the field.

So with the soft-left emasculated, the main hope for an alternative to Le Pen and Mélenchon has to be focused on the right. But here the prospects – which until recently seemed bright – are now clouded with gloom.

"A Mélenchon–Le Pen duel in round two is not yet inevitable," says Guillaume Tabard, political analyst at the conservative Le Figaro newspaper. "But it is looking increasingly probable."

In recent weeks the poll ratings of the main centre-right hopeful Edouard Philippe – a former prime minister under President Macron – have fallen sharply, and he is now consistently placed behind Mélenchon in the first round of the vote. Marine Le Pen is way ahead of both.

Other candidates for command of this centre-right "space" are circling. They include another former Macron prime minister, Gabriel Attal; the leader of the right-wing Republicans (and former Macron interior minister), Bruno Retailleau; and now – a surprise new challenger – the mayor of Cannes, David Lisnard.

Lisnard, who stands on a liberal economic platform of less state and lower taxes, has emerged from nowhere to become the man of the hour. Membership of his micro-party Nouvelle Energie (New Energy) has shot up to more than 100,000, and he is being taken seriously as a possible Philippe replacement.

But this very multiplicity of names – not to mention others like judoka Teddy Riner, journalist Natacha Polony and former prime minister Dominique de Villepin – betrays the essential weakness of the centre-right challenge.

According to veteran commentator Nicolas Baverez, "If you want to win an election, it's quite simple: you need a strategy, a programme, and activists. Right now in the space between Le Pen and Mélenchon we have none of that: there is a total vacuum.

"The most glaring absence is digital. Mélenchon especially, but Le Pen too, are running extremely effective social media campaigns. In the middle… nothing."

Guillaume Tabard agrees that the lack of a shared platform is proving a serious handicap.

"In recent weeks we have seen Marine Le Pen issue her manifesto proposals for reforming pensions. We have seen Jean-Luc Mélenchon publish his programme in a best-selling book," he says.

"What do we have in between? Arguments about names and polling figures and whether or not there should be a primary. It's not, to put it mildly, an encouraging start."

For Fressoz, "There is no-one in the centre who is taking up the fight. When Le Pen makes her proposals about pensions, there is no-one saying, 'Hang on, that doesn't add up!'. Macron – who did after all take her on and beat her – is said to be furious."

Any mention of Macron, though, is most unwelcome for the camp that nominally is his heir. Philippe, Attal and Retailleau all served under a president who Baverez now calls "as toxic as Trump", so deep is his unpopularity in the country. Lisnard, by contrast, makes much of his refusal to serve under Macron – but he faces another handicap.

According to Fressoz, "Lisnard has shot up in the polls because he is on the right of the right, and there is always an appetite for a figure who is not Le Pen, but who speaks her kind of language on immigration.

"But Lisnard is an economic liberal, and in France that is a minority taste. He'll have his moment but then he will deflate."

With five months to go to until the election, all is not lost for the mainstream. Optimists in its ranks say that come the new year, opinion polls will start settling behind one or other centre-right candidate, and the others will feel obliged to step aside.

Talk of a centre-right primary – as occurred ahead of the 2017 election – is beginning to ebb. The two strongest candidates, Philippe and Lisnard, are opposed. Lisnard says he supports one but his conditions are designed to be unacceptable to the rest. Retailleau and Attal are in favour – but that, says Tabard, is "mainly as a way to keep their hopes alive."

In theory then it is possible a name will emerge in January or February, and start pulling behind him (or less likely, her) the mass of voters who do not want a disruptive radical as France's next head of state.

For Fressoz of Le Monde, "After years of Macron's 'neither left nor right', the left and right are once again shaping French politics. But now it is the extremes who are in control."

Le Pen and Mélenchon have both already run three times for the presidency. Their visions were defined long ago, their strategies laid, their activists trained. Polarisation is their friend, so is the social tension of recent weeks, and both are undisputed masters in their own camps.

The 2027 dénouement has been in their sights for years. That is their massive advantage.

items.title: US Army says controlled blast of explosives in Iowa was 'huge success'
items.summary: Despite widespread concern from residents ahead of the blast, officials say that lead readings in the area so far have been promising.
items.content:
The US military has hailed as a "huge success" the detonation of nearly five tonnes of toxic explosives in Iowa, an operation that sparked fears of health and environmental problems across the region.

Smoke was seen rising into the sky shortly after 09:00 local time (14:00 GMT) following the explosion, as the Army declared the risk "as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible".

Plans to detonate the lead azide, a volatile compound reportedly at risk of exploding on its own, were paused several times before the blast following public outcry and legal challenges.

On Wednesday evening, the Army said that an "all clear" has been issued around the ammunition plant.

President Donald Trump said shortly after the blast that reports showed mitigation efforts "far exceeded expectations".

"The Army's controlled, mitigated detonation exceeded all expectations and was a HUGE success," Adam Telle, acting secretary of the US Army, wrote on social media.

Despite widespread concern from residents of Middletown, Iowa, ahead of the blast, officials have said that lead readings in the area so far have been promising.

In a Wednesday evening update on X, the Army said that the Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) had issued the "all clear" around the plant and that there was no airborne lead detection following the detonation.

"Post-detonation surface sampling is underway, and results will be released once complete," the Army added.

Environmental Protection Agency administrator Lee Zeldin also said on social media that in the hours after the detonation "all EPA air monitors continue to report a ZERO DETECT of airborne lead".

The explosives had been in storage for around 20 years, and degraded as part of a process known as recrystallisation - this made them more responsive to accidental detonation from friction or other movement.

No level of lead exposure is considered safe, with children and pregnant women particularly vulnerable to harmful effects.

Middletown Mayor Rodney Johnson told the BBC he felt "relieved" after the detonation.

He watched the blast from his job at a manufacturing plant eight miles (12km) away from the blast - and monitored a camera at his two-bedroom home just one mile from the detonation site.

"We did not feel anything. We did not see anything," Johnson said.

Also eight miles away from Middletown, Sandy Mabeus closed the windows and the garage at her home, brought their outdoor cat inside and hunkered down.

The family watched three separate live streams on iPads and televisions of the explosion as it happened.

"We did not feel or hear a thing here," she told the BBC, adding that she checked the videos to confirm it had actually happened.

"The waiting and wondering has not been a good thing for anybody in the area," she said. "Hopefully they had a very good result and we can just get on with things."

Iowa farmer David Vandenberg lives about 20 miles from the blast site and said he first learned of the detonation around two weeks ago. The Army Corps of Engineers took samples from his yard and pond on Tuesday.

"I was listening this morning, and I did hear a rumble about nine o'clock," he told the BBC on Wednesday, but didn't see or smell anything.

Vandenberg expects officials to return to take more samples but "was happy to see that the blast was relatively contained. "I think the effects will be minimal"

Illinois Governor JB Pritzker said on X that his state was "seeing little to no impact" from the blast. In a press release, he said he was directing state agencies to remain on standby for any "unanticipated impact".

The Iowa site is only 10 miles (16 km) from the Illinois border.

Iowa's incoming Governor-elect Rob Sand said there was "more testing to do" and called for "immediate transparency" to explain why the lead-up was "so chaotic and unclear".

Sand said that any Iowans who have been impacted in any way "must be taken care of fully, right away".

Cameron Hamilton, the Fema administrator, said there would be additional resources and testing in the coming days and weeks.

In recent weeks, the US Army scheduled and rescheduled their detonation ahead of colder winter temperatures.

It also warned locals of "potential exposure to toxic lead dust", which led to some panic. It instituted measures including an optional evacuation zone and a shelter-in-place advisory ahead of the detonation.

The Army faced pushback from residents and politicians alike and there were legal challenges to prevent the detonation from going ahead on environmental and health grounds.

But on Monday, the appeals court overturned a decision to halt the blast. It said that - while these concerns were valid - the risk from an unplanned explosion was greater.

Sheila Flynn and Kwasi Gyamfi Asiedu contributed to this report

items.title: Has global jihadism failed, or is it simply changing shape?
items.summary: Jihadist groups appear to be focusing on local issues rather than global terror. Does it signify a real change?
items.content:
Rice, pasta, sugar, cooking oil and beans are hardly what you'd expect to see in jihadist propaganda. Yet these were among the supplies that al-Qaeda's Somali branch, al-Shabab, said its "charity" had handed out to hundreds of struggling families in August, as it publicised the aid through its social media accounts and radio station.

The group, which controls large parts of rural southern and central Somalia, has been keen to show off its so-called humanitarian work throughout 2026.

"May God reward them," said a local woman in one of al-Shabab's videos.

It's all part of an effort to win over local communities and present itself as more than just a jihadist group.

A quarter of a century after al-Qaeda's 9/11 attacks in the US, and 12 years after Islamic State group (IS) declared its so-called caliphate in Iraq and Syria, the jihadist movement looks very different.

Rather than focusing on attacking the West or fighting for a global Islamic state, some - especially those linked to al-Qaeda - are putting more effort into winning power closer to home. And they seem increasingly willing to make compromises along the way.

Because of this, a debate is growing within the movement. While hardliners reject compromise, pragmatists see working with local groups and former enemies as a way to gain power. But do the pragmatists represent a genuine change or simply a shift in tactics to achieve the same ultimate goals: establishing a state that applies their strict interpretation of Islamic Sharia law both at home and in its dealings with the outside world?

Neither al-Qaeda nor IS has achieved its ultimate dream: taking over one or more countries and ruling them according to their strict interpretation of Islam.

Both have suffered major defeats, lost leaders and faced years of international pressure. IS, which once controlled vast areas of Iraq and Syria, lost its last territorial stronghold in 2019. But jihadism hasn't gone away.

Africa is now the main battleground for jihadism, with al-Qaeda's powerful branches, JNIM in the Sahel (Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger) and al-Shabab in Somalia, fighting long-running insurgencies. IS, its bitter rival, has active branches in Nigeria, the Democratic Republic of Congo, the Sahel, Mozambique and Somalia.

One major source of inspiration, and envy, whether jihadists admit it or not, is Syria's new president, Ahmed al-Sharaa . The former IS and then al-Qaeda commander was once wanted by the US but rose to power in Syria in December 2024 and was welcomed by Western leaders.

Once known by his militant nom de guerre Abu Mohammed al-Jolani, he led the jihadist group Nusra Front - initially linked to IS and then al-Qaeda - and later the group Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS).

He gradually broke ties with both IS and al-Qaeda and distanced himself from their calls for global jihad.

Instead, he focused on Syria, building a local power base in the north-western Idlib province.

What surprised everyone was his growing willingness to work with non-Islamist groups and engage with foreign powers. As HTS advanced on Damascus, its leadership sought to reassure the international community, reaching out even to Russia, a key ally of then-president Bashar al-Assad, to allay fears of an Islamist takeover.

That pragmatism, combined with favourable geopolitical conditions - including a weaker Russia and Iran - helped him take power in Syria.

But the sight of him being welcomed by world leaders, including US President Donald Trump, was even more remarkable.

During Sharaa's visit to the White House in November 2025, Trump sprayed him with his own branded cologne, jokingly asked how many wives he had and praised him as a "very strong leader".

For some jihadists, Sharaa's success has been inspiring. Others, however, see his actions as a betrayal of everything they believe in.

IS has declared jihad against Syria's new Islamist government, branding Sharaa and his officials "apostates", and has carried out attacks against government forces on that basis. Other hardline clerics have taken a similar stance, but have stopped short of openly calling for jihad against Sharaa.

The divide between hardline jihadists and their more pragmatic counterparts has fuelled a bitter online debate since 2025, with rival voices trading accusations of betrayal and even publishing competing books to defend their positions.

For hardliners, going too far can mean abandoning their core beliefs. This might include holding back from imposing their strict version of Islamic law, accepting "man-made" laws or a constitution, taking part in elections, working with non-Islamist groups, or building ties with governments they consider "infidel".

Another source of inspiration for jihadists was the Taliban's return to power in Afghanistan in 2021, as it showed that an Islamist movement could eventually take control of a country after years of fighting Western-backed forces. It engaged local groups, slowly secured power across the country, used international diplomacy, and bided its time before taking the capital, Kabul, in a lightning offensive.

Two groups are especially worth watching: al-Qaeda's branches in Mali and Somalia.

In late April, al-Qaeda's Sahel branch, known as JNIM, showed considerable pragmatism by joining forces with nationalist Tuareg separatists - whom it had occasionally fought - to launch a major offensive that threatened Mali's military rulers. It even went as far as to call the Tuaregs "brothers".

But it's not just JNIM's growing military strength that's attracting attention. It's also how the group is presenting itself.

Its propaganda once prominently featured al-Qaeda's leaders, slogans and calls for global jihad. Since late 2024, however, its videos have dropped the familiar al-Qaeda branding.

And instead of talking about global Muslim causes, JNIM has increasingly focused on local problems, portraying itself as a defender of ordinary people against corrupt and abusive rulers.

It has repeatedly accused Mali's military government and its Russian allies of killing civilians and making people's lives worse.

In April, it appealed to "all sincere patriots" to help build a "new Mali", promising security, justice and prosperity alongside Islamic law.

It has even suggested it could have "balanced relations" with Russia, despite the fact they're fighting Russian forces backing Mali's government. Its wording echoed that of HTS to Russia as it advanced on Damascus.

There are parallels with Sharaa's approach in Syria: build local alliances, reassure potential enemies and avoid giving outside powers a reason to intervene.

Africa security specialist Aman Bezreh sees similarities between the two groups, but says JNIM's shift may take time.

"JNIM has indeed shown signs of pragmatism similar to HTS", she says. "However, its rebranding has progressed more slowly because the group is simultaneously focused on expanding into new territories and recruiting from diverse pools."

The debate over which path to follow is also taking place within JNIM's leadership, according to Wassim Nasr, a France 24 journalist and jihadism expert.

He says one camp favours the Taliban's approach of taking power through force with minimal concessions. The other, which he says currently has the upper hand, favours an approach closer to that of Syria's HTS - making compromises and building wider alliances to gain power more quickly.

Nasr believes JNIM may borrow from both models, but that a break with al-Qaeda is inevitable as a result of its political evolution.

Like JNIM, al-Shabab in Somalia appears willing to make deals with former enemies.

According to Abdullahi Guji, BBC Monitoring's Somalia specialist, al-Shabab reached a truce in October with a powerful Somali tribe, the Ma'awisley, whose fighters had been at the forefront of the fight against the group.

The tribe has since withdrawn its fighters from the front line, dealing a serious blow to the government's campaign against jihadists, says Guji.

Guji believes the group may soon have a chance to test whether it can seize power and establish itself as an alternative government across wider parts of the country.

African Union forces are withdrawing from Somalia amid funding cuts and the approaching end of their mandate in December. Meanwhile, the Somali government is facing political crises and rebellions, creating vulnerabilities al-Shabab could exploit, he adds.

There's another reason some jihadists may see an opportunity to expand: they believe Western governments have bigger fish to fry.

With the war in Ukraine, US-Iran conflict in the Middle East and growing rivalries with China and Russia, fighting jihadists is no longer the priority it was after 9/11.

The US withdrawal from Afghanistan in 2021 and the Taliban's return to power, followed by Sharaa's rise in Syria, have reinforced that belief.

Colin Clarke, executive director of the Soufan Center, a non-profit research group that focuses on security, says some jihadist groups have learnt that avoiding confrontation with the US can help them escape Western military action and "live to fight another day".

items.title: A renovation was meant to improve these Hong Kong homes - it ended in a blaze that killed 168
items.summary: A year after one of Hong Kong's deadliest fires, families left behind are still waiting for justice.
items.content:
It was a sunny Wednesday afternoon on 26 November last year, and Mrs Lau was attending a dance class at an activity centre close to her home.

At around 14:45 she heard the faint sounds of fire engine sirens - but didn't think much of it.

It was only a while later, when she started receiving calls from a friend, that she found out that Wang Fuk Court - the eight-block apartment complex she had called home for the past 40 years - was ablaze. And her husband - a wheelchair user - was trapped inside their home.

"I grabbed my things quickly and ran down without even putting my shoes on properly," Mrs Lau, who wanted to be identified only by her surname, told the BBC.

When she got there, the building had been cordoned off by police.

She called her 74-year-old husband but he told her not to worry - he hadn't heard an alarm so it was probably a small fire, he said.

Mrs Lau could only watch helplessly as the blaze tore through Wang Fuk Court at a peak speed of about 10m (33ft) per second - an "unprecedented" rate, a final report released by an independent committee in relation to the deadly blaze that killed 168 people found.

It was a tragedy that was entirely preventable but happened as a result of a series of human errors, fire safety failures, alleged fraud and suspected corruption, said the report.

"It was ferocious… I saw the fire jump [from one building to another] - then a huge fireball burst. It was truly hell on Earth. How could anyone possibly escape?" said Mrs Lau.

She tried calling her husband again. This time, there was no answer.

The body of Lau Man Kwong was eventually found by rescuers - he had locked himself inside the toilet.

"He was wearing his slippers, sitting on the toilet and clutching his identity card," said his wife, who added that she escaped death "by the narrowest margin".

"He was such a good person. I just don't understand why he had to die in such a terrible way."

Mr Lau and his wife moved into Wang Fuk Court in 1983 - the year the building was completed.

She recalls an idyllic life - a family with three children who were able to grow up close to the sea and spend weekends playing at a nearby park.

"All three of my children adored my husband… He could be very stern, and I was the only woman who could make him laugh."

In Hong Kong, all buildings over 30 years old have to undergo an inspection - and any necessary renovations as a result.

Like many building complexes in Hong Kong, Wang Fuk Court had a management committee that oversaw things like building repairs. As many as 57 construction companies submitted bids. But the company that won, Prestige Construction and Engineering (PC&E), submitted the most expensive bid at HK$336m ($42.8m; £32.4m).

Residents, many of whom were over 65, had to bear the cost. The hefty bills triggered protests but eventually, the contract was signed. But once the renovations began in July 2024, residents were unhappy.

Among the complaints was that workers constantly smoked on site, dropping cigarette butts everywhere.

The 1,154 page report suggested the fire was caused by a lit cigarette.

There were also complaints about most of Wang Fuk Court's eight buildings having their windows taped over with foam boards to stop debris falling in - blocking daylight or any sort of view at all, for months.

All eight buildings were also covered in a protective mesh netting and bamboo scaffolding.

The report also found that after typhoons damaged the original scaffolding nets in 2025, cheaper non-fire-retardant replacements were chosen - something that was done as a "cost-saving measure at the expense of the safety of the residents".

Residents had filed nearly 140 complaints to six government departments, including the fire services and the buildings departments, in and after 2024, but these were largely ignored, the report went on to say.

It also revealed that a staff member of the estate's property manager, ISS, had turned off the power supply to the fire alarms in all eight buildings - which is why no alarms rang on the day itself.

ISS later told the BBC it had "reviewed and reinforced its procedures [and] staff training" in Hong Kong, adding that it takes the findings of the report "very seriously".

But for those who did manage to flee their homes - the emergency staircase turned out to be another death trap. Windows were removed from some fire escape stairwells to create temporary openings for workers - letting in smoke and cutting off vital escape routes.

Dozens, including Christy's husband, died in such stairwells.

Christy, who wanted to be identified only by her first name, says her husband was at home alone when the fire broke out. She only found out about it when her friends sent her messages about it. By the time she made it to the apartment complex, it was already cordoned off.

She found out later that he had died of smoke inhalation in the stairwell, something she says that is at least of some consolation to her.

"My husband's body would have been burnt and he would have been in more pain if he was at home. At the very least… his suffering was minimal."

Christy says her family had just celebrated their eldest child's ninth birthday the day before - they had saved some leftover cake in the fridge to eat the next day. Their father never got to eat it.

Both children have been deeply affected by the loss of their father.

Her youngest child, a seven-year-old boy, had "covered his ears and yelled" when he was first told what had happened to his father.

He now often comforts his mother, saying he will take care of her as he is the only man in the family.

"He hides his emotions. A seven-year-old child should not behave this way, and I feel heartbroken," says Christy, who has herself been diagnosed with PTSD and depression.

Her daughter has "extreme thoughts" she says, and channels her emotions through art.

She turned 10 on Wednesday, but this year, there was no birthday celebration in sight.

Her birthday, she says, will now instead be a day to commemorate her father.

Wang Fuk Court's problems date back to before the renovations began.

The management company hired to oversee and supervise the project, Will Power, conspired with PC&E to defraud residents in Wang Fuk Court, according to the city's Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC).

Although PC&E was found to have breached safety requirements and violated building department rules for multiple previous projects, homeowners at Wang Fuk Court were told that they had a clean record.

The ICAC alleges that this was part of a lucrative scheme, with Will Power's director Wong Hap-yin, along with other individuals, laundering over $5m in suspected proceeds from the tendering process from Wang Fuk Court, among other housing projects.

Once PC&E cinched the contract, Will Power's registered inspector - an individual meant to oversee the renovations - merely rubber-stamped the documents, without having actually conducted any inspections personally, the report added.

Will Power has been since liquidated and PC&E could not be reached for a response.

Both companies - Will Power and PC&E - and seven individuals have been charged with 25 counts of offences including including manslaughter, conspiracy to defraud, attempting to pervert the course of public justice and tax evasion.

Four of them are still in custody but none of the cases have gone to trial yet.

The report said both companies involved were the "main culprits responsible".

But it also directed heavy criticism at authorities, saying that "no government department took effective ownership of various fire safety issues and complaints about fire hazards fell into a vacuum".

One expert, Prof John Burns of Hong Kong University, had called the event the "largest governance crisis" that authorities have faced since 2020 - a reference to the controversial National Security Law that was passed in that year.

On the day the report was released, almost one year after the fire, Hong Kong's housing chief Winnie Ho resigned and the city's top leader John Lee apologised for the first time, promising that a "large number" of reforms would be rolled out.

Five months after the fire, Mrs Lau was allowed into her flat for the first time to collect any personal belongings that might have remained.

In her first visit, she was given just three hours to retrieve 40 years' worth of belongings.

Pictures taken from the visit show a home that has been utterly burned out - with every surface blackened and soot covering the floor.

"I almost fainted when I saw what had become of my home. I don't understand how the home I had built, such a warm and beautiful home, could end up like this," said Mrs Lau.

Her children, who came with her, described the house as a "war zone". Among the rubble, they found broken pieces of a piggy bank that Mr Lau had dutifully filled with coins every day for the past 20 years.

"Everyone in our family knew it was his favourite possession. The piggy bank died with him," said Mrs Lau.

Mrs Lau and her daughter have since rented a place nearby to live - and she is worried about how she is going to afford a new house.

items.title: Coppa Davis: l'Italia soffre ma supera la Corea e conquista la semifinale
items.summary: La vittoria col doppio di Berrettini-Vavassori, ora la sfida è con i cechi
items.content: Sessant'anni esatti dopo la storica debacle del calcio ai Mondiali del 1966, quando dopo la disfatta degli azzurri il termine "Corea" divenne sinonimo di sconfitta clamorosa e inaspettata, lo spettro di una nuova "Corea" ha aleggiato sul tennis alla BolognaFiere Arena. Ma l'Italia del tennis, pur soffrendo e lottando, ha saputo superare l'ostacolo coreano, conquistando il pass per le semifinali di Coppa Davis, dove venerdì 27 novembre affronterà la Repubblica Ceca. C'è stato bisogno del doppio e di cinque tie break per battere una squadra sulla carta nettamente inferiore. Alla fine gli azzurri hanno battuto 2-1 gli uomini del capitano Jong-Sam Chung, alla prima apparizione ai quarti, tenendo alto il morale per l'obiettivo prefissato: la conquista del quarto successo consecutivo, il secondo in casa, anche senza la propria stella Jannik Sinner. Ma la squadra di Filippo Volandri ha dovuto sudare più del previsto per piegare la resistenza coreana. La sfida, infatti, è stata lunga (iniziata alle 16 e finita oltre le 23) e combattuta. Si è aperta nel segno azzurro, con il successo nel primo singolare di Lorenzo Musetti, che si è imposto in due set su Seongchan Hong (6-0, 7-6). "Siamo tutti professionisti, credo sia questo che ci rende quelli da battere", ha esultato, rimarcando: "a questa maglia io ci tengo tantissimo". La partita però si è incrinata con la performance di Flavio Cobolli, uscito sconfitto dal match contro l'avversario: "Abbiamo lottato, ho lottato fino alla fine con il massimo delle mie forze" e "ho disputato una delle partite migliori dell'ultimo periodo contro un giocatore che non vale sicuramente la sua classifica attuale: mi ha molto sorpreso, dopo aver perso il primo set, questa sua reazione", ha confessato, parlando del sudcoreano Soonwoo Kwon, 139/o nella classifica del ranking. Cobolli ha ceduto in tre set a Kwon, al termine di una battaglia punto a punto. Alla rimonta ci hanno pensato Matteo Berrettini e Andrea Vavassori, schierati da Volandri per il doppio, contro la coppia formata da Hyeon Chung e Kwon, che fino all'ultimo non ha dato tregua: il terzo match si è chiuso in due set, entrambi tirati e decisi al tie break, con un grande sospiro di sollievo - specialmente nel secondo, con tanti set point anche per gli asiatici. Con la Repubblica Ceca, venerdì, servirà alzare il livello.

items.title: Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt settle legal battle over French winery
items.summary: The Hollywood A-listers' legal battle focused on the vineyard they bought in 2008 and where they wed six years later.
items.content:
Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie have settled a long-running legal battle over her sale of a stake in their French vineyard, which unfolded amid a bitter divorce.

"We have settled out of court in the best interests of our family and will not be commenting further," said the Hollywood stars' representatives in a joint statement.

They bought a controlling interest in Château Miraval in 2008 and wed there six years later.

In the lawsuit, Pitt , 62 , argued that Jolie, 51, acted without his permission in selling her share in the winery to a Russian oligarch. She counter-sued, accusing Pitt of drunkenly attacking her and their children on a flight, prompting her to file for divorce in 2016.

The settlement announced on Wednesday resolves both of their respective legal actions.

"Any comments in media stories attributed to 'sources' are in fact not coming from either of us, or anyone close to us," said the statement from their representatives.

Pitt's lawsuit had accused Jolie of seeking "to inflict harm" on him when she sold her stake in their co-owned vineyard, which he claimed had forced him to partner with "a stranger with poisonous associations and intentions".

The Fight Club star said he and Jolie had agreed not to sell their stakes in the venue without the permission of the other.

It was alleged that Jolie had sold her share to a Luxembourg-based spirits manufacturer controlled by Russian oligarch Yuri Shefler, without Pitt's knowledge.

Jolie hit back with her own lawsuit, accusing Pitt of grabbing her by the head and attacking two of their children during a 2016 private jet flight trip.

Pitt also verbally abused and poured alcohol on his family during the flight from France to Los Angeles, her lawsuit had alleged.

Her lawyers alleged Pitt began shouting, accusing her of being "too deferential" to their six children - aged eight to 15 at the time.

Pitt was not charged following a police investigation into the incident and he denied the allegations.

They reached a divorce settlement late last year after an eight-year legal battle.

It is understood that Pitt's litigation with Stoli Group, a beverage company owned by the Russian oligarch, is ongoing.

At the time of their 2014 marriage, Pitt and Jolie were among the most lucrative names in Hollywood.

They met on the set of the 2005 film Mr and Mrs Smith and were soon dubbed Brangelina by the press.

The marriage was Pitt's second after a relationship with Friends star Jennifer Aniston.

It was Jolie's third, after actors Billy Bob Thornton and Jonny Lee Miller.

Jolie adopted her first child, Maddox, from Cambodia in 2002 a few months after he was born. Pitt later adopted him after he and Jolie had begun their relationship.

In 2005, the pair adopted daughter Zahara from Ethiopia when she was a few months old.

The couple's first biological child, Shiloh, was born in Namibia in 2006.

Their son Pax was adopted at the age of three from Vietnam in 2007, and twins Knox and Vivienne were born in 2008.

Since the couple split, four of the six children have legally changed their last name to Jolie rather than Jolie-Pitt, according to court filings citied by Hollywood press.

items.title: Morto Andy Taylor, ex chitarrista dei Duran Duran
items.summary: Aveva 65 anni, nel 2018 la diagnosi di cancro alla prostata
items.content:
E' morto a 65 anni Andy Taylor, ex chitarrista dei Duran Duran. Lo riporta il Guardian. Nel 2018 gli era stato diagnosticato un cancro alla prostata metastatico al quarto stadio, notizia che rese pubblica nel 2022, quando i Duran Duran stavano per essere inseriti nella Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

Andy Taylor è morto lunedì 23 novembre nella sua casa londinese, ma la notizia è stata resa nota solo oggi dalla famiglia e dalla stessa band, simbolo della new wave degli anni '80, in un comunicato. "Andy Taylor, amato marito, padre e nonno, è scomparso dopo una lunga e coraggiosa battaglia contro un cancro alla prostata. Aveva 65 anni. Andy si è spento serenamente nella sua casa, circondato dai suoi cari, lunedì 23 novembre", si legge nella nota pubblicata sull'account Instagram e sul sito web del gruppo. "Ha affrontato questi ultimi anni con grande coraggio e determinazione.

Non ha mai smesso di lottare, fino all'ultimo istante, senza mai perdere il suo amore per la vita", ha dichiarato la moglie Tracey. I membri del gruppo hanno elogiato "il fuoco e la spavalderia indelebili" che ha apportato alla band. Nato il 16 febbraio 1961 nel nord-est dell'Inghilterra, Andy Taylor si unì ai Duran Duran a Birmingham nell'aprile del 1980, all'età di 19 anni.

La sua chitarra ha caratterizzato i primi tre album del gruppo, dal 1981 al 1983. Il primo singolo, "Planet Earth", raggiunse la dodicesima posizione in classifica. Ma fu il loro terzo singolo, "Girls on Film" - accompagnato da un video audace che mostrava donne a seno nudo intente a lottare nel fango - a catapultare i Duran Duran verso la fama mondiale. Tuttavia a metà degli anni '80, emersero dei dissidi all'interno della formazione. Andy Taylor si dedicò quindi ad altri progetti, tra cui il gruppo The Power Station, avviando parallelamente anche una carriera da solista. Rientrato nel gruppo nel 2000, lo lasciò di nuovo nel 2006 a causa di divergenze. Alla fine del 2022, l'ingresso dei Duran Duran nella Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, negli Stati Uniti, avrebbe dovuto segnare una reunion con Andy Taylor: durante la cerimonia di premiazione a Los Angeles, il cantante Simon Le Bon lesse una lettera in cui Taylor spiegava di aver ricevuto una diagnosi di cancro alla prostata metastatico al quarto stadio. Lascia la moglie Tracey e i figli Andrew, Isabelle, Bethany e Georgina.

items.title: Sucic e Lautaro, l'Inter torna a vincere in Champions
items.summary: Nove punti in classifica, risposta dei nerazzurri dopo il pari a Bergamo
items.content: L'Inter non sbaglia la prova Champions League e torna a vincere dopo il pari contro l'Atalanta che aveva alimentato tante critiche. Contro lo Stoccarda, sblocca Sucic su rigore, poi sigilla Lautaro Martinez a cui bastano 6' per entrare e segnare. I nerazzurri si portano a 9 punti in classifica, al dodicesimo posto e tra l'altro scavalcano proprio gli avversari della serata. L'approccio alla partita è migliore per lo Stoccarda che mette in difficoltà l'Inter con un pressing alto che ne limita l'intraprendenza. La squadra di Chivu fatica ad impostare e costruire, così sono i tedeschi a farsi pericolosi. Al 6' traversone velenoso dello Stoccarda non impattato per un soffio da Demirovic. Altra buona occasione per l'attaccante non sfruttata pochi minuti dopo. Al 15' viene chiamato in causa Martinez da una conclusione di Fuehrich da posizione ravvicinata. Poi l'Inter prende le misure, capisce di dover allargare maggiormente la manovra e iniziano a fioccare le occasioni da gol. Una delle più nitide della prima parte della partita l'ha Spence, che davanti alla porta, a tu per tu con Seimen, gli calcia addosso. Al 24' angolo per l'Inter con Bisseck che allunga per Akanji ma lo svizzero arriva in ritardo. Con il passare del tempo i nerazzurri conquistano campo, ritmo e gioco, manca però cinismo sotto porta. Al 40' un problema fisico alla coscia sinistra obbliga Bastoni a chiedere il cambio, entra Dimarco al suo posto. E proprio nei minuti finali, arrivano le due occasioni più nette: Jeltsch sbaglia tutto con un retropassaggio che di fatto lancia Thuram, ma il francese a tu per tu con il portiere sbaglia tutto e calcia di poco a lato scheggiando il palo esterno. Neanche il tempo di disperarsi e altra clamorosa chance pr l'Inter ma in questo caso il portiere dello Stoccarda neutralizza con un salvataggio provvidenziale: tiro d'esterno di Barella, palla che colpisce il legno e viene poi intercettato da Seimen. Al 10' della ripresa, l'episodio che sblocca la partita. Dimarco dalla sinistra crossa al centro, intercetta palla Vagnoman con il braccio largo e dopo un rapido consulto delle immagini al Var, l'arbitro indica il dischetto. Prende palla Sucic che non sbaglia come già accaduto a Bergamo domenica scorsa. Gli ospiti però non demordono e al 21' è provvidenziale l'intervento di Carlos Augusto Su Demirovic. Uno spavento che porta ad una reazione di Chivu. Il tecnico richiama Thuram, stanchissimo, e inserisce Lautaro Martinez. E' il 26', all'argentino bastano 6' per fare - come sempre - la differenza. Ripartenza Inter, Dimarco tiene palla sinistra, Lautaro chiede di essere servito, poi controlla e calcia velocissimo spiazzando il portiere dello Stoccarda. E' raddoppio e l'ennesima prova di come l'argentino riesca ad incidere in una manciata di minuti. Aver recuperato il capitano è probabilmente la miglior notizia per Chivu e per tutto l'ambiente. Funziona bene l'Inter questa volta. Anche la difesa esce dal campo con un clean sheet che è rincuorante viste le ultime statistiche. Martinez, non al meglio per un colpo preso nella ripresa, esce da imbattuto grazie anche agli interventi provvidenziali di Akanji e Carlos Augusto. L'Inter dà la risposta che tutti si aspettavano e rilancia il percorso europeo allontanando definitivamente le critiche definite "disfattiste" da Barella alla vigilia.

items.title: Thirty-one killed in massive fire as fuel tanker crashes on Cairo highway
items.summary: Another 21 are injured after the tanker reportedly overturns on a busy ring road in the Egyptian capital.
items.content:
Thirty-one people have been killed and 21 others injured in a large fire on a busy highway in Cairo after a fuel tanker crashed, Egypt's health ministry says.

Hospitals nearby treated patients suffering burns and smoke inhalation after the incident, which occurred on a section of a ring road in the Warraq neighbourhood, to the north of the old city centre, on Wednesday evening.

Footage circulating on social media showed billowing flames and black smoke towering high into the night sky, with multiple nearby vehicles torched.

Officials have not given an account of how the fire broke out, but state-owned media reported the tanker had overturned, dousing nearby vehicles with petrol.

The regional public prosecutor has launched an investigation into the incident and asked that DNA samples be taken from bodies of the dead.

The tanker, which belonged to a private contractor, had been travelling along the highway when a high-voltage cable fell in front of it, prompting the driver to lose control, Al-Ahram reports, citing sources with knowledge of the investigation.

It then crossed the central reservation, overturned and caught fire, the state-owned newspaper says.

Egypt has suffered several deadly fires in recent years, with informal residential areas and often run-down infrastructure making incidents more common, the response to which is often complicated by slow emergency response times and locally improvised rescue efforts, even in the sprawling Egyptian capital.

Images from the scene show a large crowd gathered on the highway after the fire had been extinguished, as emergency services blocked off entry routes.

The health ministry said 39 ambulances had been dispatched to respond to the fire, while it posted images of Egypt's health minister overseeing the treatment of the injured at one of Cairo's hospitals.

Road collisions are also common in Egypt, often attributed to lax maintenance and the widespread flouting of traffic laws.

Nearly 6,000 people died on Egypt's roads last year, official figures show, a rise of several hundred on the previous year's total.

Emergency responders have since cleared the highway and allowed it to reopen, state broadcaster NMA reports.

A bulldozer could earlier be seen at the scene clearing the burnt-out wrecks of cars.

items.title: Bare Metal Qwen
items.summary: Article URL: https://github.com/alesha-pro/llm.asm/tree/main/02-baremetal-os Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50648365 Points: 87 # Comments: 16
items.content:
A standalone bootable x86-64 operating system that runs Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B directly on hardware or KVM with no Linux, no Windows, no C, no Rust, and no libc .

Running live on a diskless ( 0 GB storage) Proxmox VE VM booted from the hybrid BIOS+UEFI ISO (Intel Xeon E5-2670 v3, 12 cores, 2 GiB RAM):

From the repository root ( FAST_Q8=1 is enabled by default; pass FAST_Q8=0 for legacy FP32-activation mode):

(The kernel is linked as 64-bit ELF and wrapped into ELF32 via objcopy -O elf32-i386 for standard Multiboot 1 loaders like QEMU -kernel and GRUB2; boot.asm transitions immediately into 64-bit Long Mode.)

Boot directly in the terminal over COM1 serial ( -nographic ):

Packages the 23 KB kernel, GRUB2 Multiboot 1 config, and the 649 MiB .asmbin model into a single self-contained ~661 MiB bootable ISO ( build/asm-llm-os.iso ):

Because the entire OS and model live inside the ISO and run out of RAM, the VM needs zero hard disks .

(Note: --cpu host is required so the VM exposes AVX2 + FMA, and --balloon 0 ensures 2 GiB of contiguous guest RAM for the 649 MiB model + 449 MiB KV-cache arena.)

By default, the bare-metal console runs in multi-turn chat mode with persistent KV-cache : each new user turn prefills only the new Qwen3 chat tokens starting at g_chat_pos without recomputing earlier turns, closes every assistant turn in the KV-cache with \n , and displays live context usage ( ctx=X/2048 ) in the decode stats line. When the KV-cache approaches max_seq ( pos + n_prompt + 64 >= max_seq ), it prints [chat] context full, resetting KV-cache and resets cleanly. If booted with prompt="..." and shutdown=0 , the initial batch turn stays in the KV-cache so you can continue the same conversation in the REPL.

Both PS/2 keyboard (VGA) and COM1 serial ( 115200 8N1 ) are polled simultaneously. Type any message and press Enter, or use a built-in command:

Pass via QEMU -append "..." , make os-run CMDLINE='...' , or make os-iso CMDLINE='...' :

Phase 2 compiles the exact same shared/math.asm , shared/matmul.asm , shared/tokenizer.asm , and shared/transformer.asm with -DBARE_METAL -DFAST_Q8=$(FAST_Q8) and pairs them with 4,167 lines of bare-metal OS code:

All 5 parity prompts (English technical, English concise, Russian UTF-8, arithmetic word problem, --think mode) match Phase 1 ( build/asm-llm ) 100% exact in prompt tokens, generated tokens, and raw UTF-8 bytes.

(Because boot.asm identity-maps guest RAM with 2 MiB huge pages, the bare-metal kernel avoids 4 KiB page-table walks across the 614 MiB model and outperforms both Linux mmap() Phase 1 and llama.cpp CPU Q8_0 at every thread count.)

items.title: Deploying a payphone on a tiny Pacific Island
items.summary: Article URL: https://nickvsnetworking.com/deploying-a-payphone-on-a-tiny-pacific-island-for-fun-and-zero-profit/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50648323 Points: 55 # Comments: 7
items.content:
For the past few years Australia’s Telstra has run a campaign of “Free calls to Santa” from the universal service obligation funded payphones across the country – It’s a really fun idea and we wanted to replicate it on our network on Norfolk Island where we run the mobile network, but the’s no payphones.*

* There is now a payphone – You probably already guessed this.

Those who have seen my office / shed / studio / the HackHouse, know that I may have one or two payphones… But this needed a payphone that could stand the elements and be modern ish.

The answer, is of course, to use the sexiest payphone of all time; the Nortel Millennium . Featuring VFD display, durable keypad, card service, coin service, no fancy metering line required.

Unfortunately Nortel’s bankruptcy in 2008 meant I couldn’t phone up an account manager, but with the hookup of some guy with a U-Haul van full of Millennium’s in the US and a bit of a road trip, Cody from our team managed to pickup some really clean GTE branded payphones for the job.

Then Cody flew to Sydney where we drove to the house of someone who was heading to Norfolk the next day to explain they’d need to leave all their baggage at home as all of their baggage allowance was to be taken up with the weight of a payphone – Thanks Paul.

Eventually with the Payphone on Norfolk, we needed to get it programmed; for that there’s Howard Harte’s great mm_manager , which, with the aid of a USB modem is able to program the phones.

Sidebar: I also got this working with a softmodem (A fork of D-Modem with some minor tweaks I’ve documented here ), so we could do it via straight SIP without the USB modem required – but the USB modem was the easier path.

The Philtel blog post covers how to setup your Millennium if you’re looking to play along at home yourself.

I hit a bit of a stumbling block with mm_manager as the software assumed you were part of the North American Numbering Plan (NANP) – as one of the literally dozens of people who live outside of America, having to put a 1 in front of the number wasn’t going to fly.

After some trial and error I sussed out what bits on the config files that get pushed to the phone controls this and submitted a PR to mm_manager which is now merged.

We’re also able to set the messaging that appears on the screen, which I’m very happy with the branding on.

We set it for free-on-net calls, so anyone can call any Norfone number without charge and the Payphone tag number.

Once this would’ve been the hard part, I did some work a long time ago with IBM Watson and built some stuff to annoy voters via phone with automated phone calls and capture their human responses and sort them and play the appropriate response. But tech has come a long way since 2019, and this was the easy part of the project.

We setup the payphone to make HOHOHO (464646) a destination that did not require coins when we did the rating table setup when programming the phone.

The ATA the payphone is connected to just comes through to our IMS like any other fixed line subscriber; the TAS is setup to zero-rate the destination and then it’s dialplan forwards it to “Santa Bridge” listening for SIP on port 5090.

I’ve got 4 pre-recorded “Norfolk Specific” greetings to buy us time to get everything setup in the background, once these greetings play (each ends asking the caller their name) then we feed into the OpenAI API.

One of the members from our team attempted to ask Santa to write a Python script to iterate over a for loop , while another team member asked Santa for firearms. In both cases it did a good job of redirecting.

The phone came GTE branded, so we needed to redo the card with the branding on it that goes around the screen. Two screws and some wiggling later we pulled out the card, and then I badgered my partner into using their day off to design a new one, with a retro style I really like.

The install was beautifully completed by long-time-reader-of-the-blog Minas from Shield Electrical and Air.

He knocked up a housing to Shield it from the rain and elements and installed it outside the office entrance.

The last step of the puzzle was making the phone so it could be captured by cult game Payphone Tag – I reached out to Alex and gave him the info, and now it’s there in the map for anyone to capture .

So with this now in place, we’ve still got to give it some tinsel and Christmas cheer, and I’ll get some more pics of it in place.

We’re waiting for someone to claim it on Payphone tag, and we’ve shipped 3 of these to another even more remote Island I’ll hopefully be able to share more info on later.

items.title: Andy Taylor, morto l’ex chitarrista dei Duran Duran. Era l’anima rock della band
items.summary: Il musicista è scomparso dopo una lunga malattia lunedì 23 novembre. L’annuncio della famiglia e della band
items.content:
C’era anche Andy Taylor quando il mondo era conquistato dai Duran Duran . Andy è morto a 65 anni, dopo una lunga malattia: nel 2018 gli era stato diagnosticato un cancro alla prostata metastatico al quarto stadio, notizia che rese pubblica nel 2022, quando i Duran Duran stavano per essere inseriti nella Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

Quando entrò a far parte dei Duran, nel 1980, il chitarrista di Cullercoats, Gran Bretagna, aveva già alle spalle una lunga esperienza di live con band cui si era unito in giovanissima età. Dopo aver pubblicato un annuncio offrendosi come chitarrista sulla rivista Melody Maker , Taylor si recò a Birmingham per un’audizione. «Qualche giorno dopo mi chiamarono per dirmi che, tra i circa 40 candidati, ero stato l’unico capace non solo di suonare, ma persino di accordare lo strumento», avrebbe raccontato in seguito. Era il nucleo originario dei Duran Duran: un mese dopo di lui anche Simon Le Bon entrò a far parte della band. Nel febbraio 1981 pubblicarono il loro singolo d’esordio, Planet Earth , e con l’uscita di Girls on Film nel luglio dello stesso anno – brano trainato dallo stile ritmico e precisissimo di Taylor – divennero grandi star sia nel Regno Unito che negli Stati Uniti. Rio , il loro secondo album pubblicato nel 1982, consolidò la loro immagine di playboy internazionali, raggiungendo la Top 10 in entrambi i Paesi.

In un’intervista nel 1983, Taylor descrisse la sua nuova carriera come «un hobby sfuggito al controllo». Quello stesso anno, Taylor aprì un wine bar chiamato Rio a Whitley Bay, nella sua terra natale. Dopo il terzo album, i Duran Duran si presero una breve pausa, durante la quale Taylor e il bassista John Taylor (senza alcun legame di parentela) formarono un nuovo gruppo funk-rock, i Power Station, insieme a Robert Palmer e all’ex batterista degli Chic, Tony Thompson. Andy si mostrò più volte insofferente rispetto allo stile synth-pop dei Duran: «Ero arrivato a un passo dal crollo nervoso, a causa dello stress della nostra vita folle e del mio problema con la cocaina», aveva raccontato, «Se a questo si aggiungono le continue litigate e i silenzi gelidi, era chiaro che dovevo andarmene. Il giorno dopo il Live Aid, smisi di bere e di fare uso di droghe. E iniziai, con discrezione, a chiedere consulenza legale per svincolarmi dai Duran». Il chitarrista continuò a lavorare da solista, poi nel 2001 si riunì alla band. La collaborazione finì nel 2006. La band lo ricorda con affetto: «Grazie al suo spirito pungente – unito a una visione della vita concreta, pragmatica e priva di inutili sentimentalismi – ha saputo mantenerci con i piedi per terra».

items.title: North Korea expels Swiss diplomat in sanctions row
items.summary: Swiss officials said relations would be kept through North Korea's embassy in Bern, and its own embassy in Beijing.
items.content:
North Korea has ordered Switzerland's diplomatic representative to leave the country within 48 hours and called for the office to close, in a row over sanctions.

It followed Switzerland's decision to place sanctions on the Songdowon international children's camp in the eastern city of Wonsan, which is attended by Russian and Chinese children among other nationalities.

The camp has been accused of involvement in transferring children from Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine.

North Korea's state-run news agency KCNA called the sanctions "a blatant hostile act".

Switzerland is one of the few Western nations to maintain dialogue with Pyongyang.

Confirming the expulsion, KCNA said: "The Foreign Ministry of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) declared the head of the Swiss Diplomatic Office in the DPRK persona non grata and urged him to leave the country within 48 hours."

The diplomatic rebuke comes weeks after Swiss foreign minister Ignazio Cassis made a rare visit to North Korea, where he officially reopened the office and discussed normalising relations.

Swiss authorities said relations between the two countries would be maintained through the North Korean embassy in Bern, and the Swiss embassy in Beijing.

Diplomatic links with North Korea were first established in 1974 and Switzerland opened a co-operation office in Pyongyang in 1997. It was closed during the pandemic and remained shut for six years.

Switzerland's department of foreign affairs said the country "distinguishes between its sanctions policy and its commitment to maintaining dialogue with all countries".

It added: "The reopening of the office in Pyongyang did not in any way affect Switzerland's implementation of UN sanctions related to North Korea's nuclear programme, nor its implementation of EU sanctions targeting North Korea in the context of Russia's war against Ukraine."

Thousands of North Korean soldiers have been deployed to help support Russia's war with Ukraine.

In August, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Moscow of using North Korean missiles.

Russia using North Korean missiles to strike Ukraine, Zelensky says

North Korean weapons are killing Ukrainians. The implications are far bigger

items.content:
Research artifact. Not maintained and not accepting contributions.

A Lean 4 proof of the Riemann Hypothesis and of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions, built on Mathlib and using only the axioms propext , Classical.choice and Quot.sound .

The proof is based on Levent Alpöge's, with Claude ( https://alpo.ge/remark.pdf ). This repository is a shorter version, produced in collaboration with my colleagues at Anthropic, and Claude.

Needs Lean v4.35.0 and Mathlib at commit 56a00585. In either folder:

A build takes one to two hours on 12 cores with 24 GB of memory (about 85 minutes more if the Mathlib cache is missing).

The proof has passed machine checks only, listed in each folder's README. No mathematician has read it through, and no paper comes with it.
